name: 179. Governance routing: what a virtual key may use, load balancing, key restrictions, limits and budgets (governance-routing)
description:
Wire-level pins for what governance does to routing. Each row creates its own virtual key, and where it needs them its own run-scoped OpenAI-backed providers, team and header-gated rule; dead keys carry a value OpenAI refuses for free.

Rows: (1) a provider config with allowed_models [] allows no model and is refused with model_blocked; (2) a routing rule targeting a provider the virtual key does not allow is refused with provider_blocked rather than widening the key; (3) load balancing picks the weight-1 provider and attaches the weight-0 one as a fallback, which serves when the first fails; (4) a caller's own fallbacks replace the ones load balancing would attach: the caller's fallback serves, and with it dead load balancing's live provider is not tried; (5) a provider config's key_ids restrict which key serves; (6) a request rate limit of one counts a streamed request, and the second stream is refused with 429; (7) a team budget of a fraction of a cent lets the first request through and refuses the next with 402. (8) a session bound to the weighted provider keeps it and its key until the provider's budget is spent (the run prices the provider through a pricing override, since a run-scoped provider has no price); load balancing then leaves it out, the session drops the binding and rebinds to the weight-0 provider that served, and stays there once the limit is raised; (9) a provider added to a virtual key mid-session leaves the bound session on its provider, while 592 new sessions split three ways, checked by chi-square and per-provider bands at about one false failure in a million. (10) a session binds to whichever of three equally weighted providers serves its first turn and follows it for ten more turns, with the trail naming the session; (11) a session bound to a moves to its weight-0 fallback b when a's key fails, serves on b as the primary from then on, and is not won back once a's key works again although load balancing picks a; (12) a session bound to b stays there after the weights move to a while b remains in the chain at weight 0; once b's weight is removed the binding is dropped, a serves and the session stays on a after b's weight is back; (13) a session bound to openai moves to b once openai's provider budget of a fraction of a cent is spent, with the trail naming the budget exclusion, and stays on b after the budget is raised; (14) a request governance refuses with 429 on the virtual key's own request limit drops the session's binding to a, so after the limit is restored the session follows load balancing to b; (15) a's only key fails on every request and b, attached as the weight-0 fallback, serves on b2, the key the virtual key's key_ids allow, though b1 weighs nine times more; (16) a provider added to a virtual key is balanced from the very next request, whose trail lists two weighted providers, and 393 requests split about evenly across both, checked by chi-square at p > 1e-6; (17) a provider removed from a virtual key stops serving from the next request, whose trail lists a alone, and a request naming it is refused with 403 provider_blocked; (18) swapping the weights of a virtual key moves the very next requests to the newly weighted provider (the split itself is pinned by the Go chi-square tests); (19) a provider deleted from Bifrost disappears from the virtual key's provider configs, and the next requests balance across what is left, each served by a as the primary; (20) governance refines the model for the provider it picks: a bare gpt-4o-mini goes to openrouter as openai/gpt-4o-mini, both as the attached fallback and as the primary, while the run's own provider keeps the bare name (governance refines only nested-slug providers and Databricks, so this row runs in the openrouter fork); (21) a session bound to c, which only the caller's own fallbacks put in the chain, keeps c first for four more turns once a and b, which load balancing picks, work again; (22) a rule targeting a with fallbacks b and c: a fails, governance refuses b on its provider request limit, which the setup spent, and c serves as fallback 2; (23) a direct key under a virtual key whose key_ids allow only a1 still goes upstream (OpenAI refuses the throwaway key with its own 401), the pool serves on a1 without it, a working direct key (the runner's openaiKey) is served on a and billed to the virtual key, and that request counts against the key's request limit of two, so the next request, direct key or not, is refused with 429; (24) on a streamed chat request, /v1/responses, /openai/v1/chat/completions and /anthropic/v1/messages, a session binds to the provider of its first turn among three equal weights and follows it for three more turns; (25) on the same four surfaces, a's dead key sends turn 1 to b, the weight-0 fallback, before any event is streamed, and turn 2 of the same session starts on b. (26) with one weighted provider among three, every bare request goes to it, the trail names the two unweighted ones as excluded, and no fallback is attached, so a refused key's 401 reaches the caller; (27) with every weight zero, the first configured provider is picked every time and the other attached as its fallback, which serves once the first fails; (28) a model naming an allowed but unweighted provider skips load balancing and is served there on its own keys with no fallbacks; (29) a provider whose budget is spent (priced through a pricing override, since a run-scoped provider has no price), and separately one whose request limit is spent, serves none of 100 bare requests, as primary or fallback, and the trail names why; (30) 1015 sessions under a 70/30 virtual key split their first turns 70/30 within a 5.1-standard-deviation band and chi-square at p > 1e-6, and every session's next two turns follow its first; (31) a provider removed from the virtual key under a bound session drops the binding, the provider that serves rebinds, and the session holds it once routing prefers another. Each row deletes what it made. Run with FEATURE="governance-routing".
